newsitem.title: UK: BOE UNLIKELY TO MAKE HABIT OF TALKING ABOUT STG.
newsitem.headline: BOE UNLIKELY TO MAKE HABIT OF TALKING ABOUT STG.

text.p: The Bank of England is unlikely to make a habit of trying to talk sterling up or down, despite its apparently successful venture into this territory on Thursday, economists said.

Currency traders responded vigorously to the Bank's hint when raising interest rates on Thursday that no further increases were imminent. Sterling was down at 2.9268/78 deutschemarks on Friday afternoon from around 3.01 marks before the Bank's statement on Thursday.

But economists said that even though the Bank's remit from the new Labour government includes supporting the government's economic policy, Thursday's remarks should not be interpreted as in any way softening its focus on its primary goal of delivering stable prices.

Alison Cottrell, chief international economist at Paine Webber International, says it was a clever move on the Bank's part to accompany the rise in official rates to 7.0 percent from 6.75 -- the fourth quarter-point move in as many months -- with a carefully worded statement to calm the markets.
The Bank said: "Upward pressures on the exchange rate should be reduced by the perception that interest rates have reached a level consistent with the inflation target."
"They did not say 'We are doing this because we want the pound to go down'," Cottrell said. "But they removed the possibility of another imminent rate hike and the pound fell."
The Bank has only been free to set interest rates since May. Its advice to raise rates had been previously been ignored for months by the former Conservative government.
"The Bank of England has only now got to where it feels happy, its neutral starting point with interest rates," Cottrell said.

"They moved in slow steps but this built the expectation that they would do another small step every time, so they've said 'In case you are worried, we think we've got to where we want to be now.' It's quite comforting in a way, because it implies that had they thought they needed a half-point increase, they would have done it."
David Philpotts, an economist at Schroders, doubts that the Bank was acting in a particularly calculated way on Thursday.

"They just thought we've had a significant tightening now and the rise in sterling since the election has applied a further tightening in monetary policy. That may well be enough. We'll wait a few months and see what happens."
The new monetary policy committee has not closed off any options in the coming months, however.

"Ironically, their statement talking sterling down -- if it is successful beyond more than just the next few days -- will put them in a position where it will be easier to raise rates later in the year," Philpotts said.

A Reuters poll of 26 London-based economists on Friday showed 17 expect further rate increases. Estimates for the peak in the current cycle ranged as high as 8.5 percent. (Details of the poll can be found on POLL1 ).
Philpotts said the Bank's comments had had the desired effect so far. Its main function remained to ensure low inflation but it was "not the Bank's job to hammer the economy," he added.

"It does suggest that they are only going to raise rates again, or even lower them, in the light of new information. Sterling is trending lower in the wake of this statement, but it doesn't look as if it is going to collapse to a level that might threaten the inflation target."
Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse, said the Bank should avoid getting involved in the debate over an appropriate level for sterling.
"I think there is a great danger that when policy-makers get involved in the currency markets, they come off worst," he said.

"They simply have to assume that if they are doing the right thing in terms of domestic economic policy, then eventually the level of the exchange rate will be appropriate. My view is that the currency has to be allowed to find its own level and policy has to be set to equate demand growth with potential supply." -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 2774
